I've farmed these 8 mu in Quzhou for 50 years now, and at 76, my back reminds me every morning that I'm not the man I was at 30. But the agricultural college training I received all those years ago still serves me well — I understand soil fertility and crop physiology, even if my body can't always execute what my mind knows is optimal.

With just my wife and me living on the farm, and our son working in a factory in Shijiazhuang, labor is my biggest constraint this year. I can't bend over picking cotton for hours anymore, and carrying 50-kilogram fertilizer bags up the field is getting difficult. So I've had to be strategic about how I allocate my 8 mu.

I'm keeping 5 mu in wheat-maize double cropping — it's the foundation of our food security and cash income. The other 3 mu stays in cotton. I've thought seriously about dropping the cotton because it's brutally labor-intensive, especially the hand-picking at my age. But lint prices have been stable around 15 yuan per jin, and those 3 mu generate more net cash per mu than the grain crops. The tradeoff is that I have to hire local women for the picking, which costs me about 1,200 yuan in hired labor. I figure the margin is still positive, but it's getting thinner every year as my own capacity diminishes.

For the winter wheat on the 5 mu, I'm planting Jimai 22 around October 12th if soil moisture permits — it's a reliable improved variety with good drought tolerance and stable yields around 480 kg/mu. Based on the soil conditions and my yield target, I'm applying 18 kg N per mu total: 10 kg as compound fertilizer in the base application before planting, and 8 kg as urea topdressed at the jointing stage next March. I learned long ago that split application is more efficient than dumping everything at once, and at my age I can't afford to waste money on fertilizer that leaches away. I'll also apply 8 kg P₂O₅ and 5 kg K₂O as base fertilizer — the phosphorus builds soil fertility over time, and the potassium helps with drought resistance. Irrigation will be four times: after planting if October is dry, at jointing in March, at heading in April, and a final irrigation at grain filling in May. Each irrigation costs about 25 yuan per mu in electricity for pumping, so that's 500 yuan just for wheat water. I'll apply a pre-emergence herbicide and monitor for fungal diseases in spring — if the weather turns wet, I'll spray a fungicide at flag leaf stage.

The summer maize goes in immediately after wheat harvest in early June — sometimes within 24 hours if the custom combine operator shows up on time. With the tight turnaround, there's no time for tillage; I'll direct-seed Zhengdan 958, a hybrid I've used for years, into the wheat stubble. I'm targeting 520 kg/mu. For fertilizer, 16 kg N per mu split between a compound base at planting and urea at the big trumpet stage when the plants have 8–10 leaves. Two irrigations: one if early summer is dry, and a critical one at tasseling-silking in late July or early August. Missing that irrigation would cost me 100 kg per mu in yield, so I budget for it even if the summer looks rainy.

For cotton on the 3 mu, I'm planting in late April after spring plowing and harrowing. I'm using an improved variety — not the most expensive hybrid, but one that performs consistently in our area. Cotton is sensitive to excess nitrogen, so I'm holding to 12 kg N per mu: a base application of compound fertilizer and a topdress at flowering. I'll irrigate twice, at flowering and at boll development. The real cost is labor. I can manage the planting, fertilizing, and spraying myself with my wife's help, but the picking requires 15 days of hired labor. At 80 yuan per day, that's 1,200 yuan. It's my biggest single expense for cotton, but without it, the bolls would rot in the fields. I'm expecting about 260 kg lint per mu if the bollworm pressure isn't too bad this year.

Total input costs will run about 5,800 yuan across all three crops. That's a significant outlay for 8 mu, but my son sends 2,000 yuan a month from Shijiazhuang, which gives us the liquidity to invest in inputs. Without that off-farm income, I'd have to cut back on fertilizer and irrigation, which would cost me yield and income. That's the reality of smallholder farming today — the farm survives because of the factory job in the city.
